readerTitle: Pay engineers for tickets, and you'll get tickets
caseNote: 가상 사례 (대기업 안의 엔지니어링 팀, 유통 물류센터) + 일화 (Apple Lisa 팀의 '−2000줄' 이야기)
insight: 엔지니어 보너스는 '무엇을 세느냐'와 '누가 어떤 규칙으로 받느냐' 두 가지를 함께 설계해야 한다. 셀 수 있는 산출물에 돈을 걸면 결과가 아니라 숫자가 움직인다.
misconception: 엔지니어에게 처리한 티켓이나 출시한 기능 수만큼 보너스를 주면 더 빨리, 더 많이 일한다.

sources.text: Andy Hertzfeld, "-2000 Lines Of Code", folklore.org (Apple Macintosh/Lisa 개발 일화 모음)
엔지니어링 팀, 물류센터 사례와 금액은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: '−2000줄' 일화: Hertzfeld의 folklore.org 글에 따르면 1982년 초 Lisa 팀 관리자들이 주간 코드 줄 수 보고를 요구했고, Bill Atkinson이 QuickDraw 영역 계산 코드를 단순화하며 약 2,000줄을 줄인 뒤 양식에 −2000이라고 적었으며, 몇 주 뒤 관리자들이 그에게 양식 제출을 더 요구하지 않았다고 합니다. 연도와 세부 내용, URL을 게시 전에 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 일화로 표시했습니다.
보너스 풀 $60,000, 엔지니어 12명 등 모든 금액과 인원은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산이 필요한 주장은 넣지 않았습니다.
3번 카드의 '티켓 쪼개기, 코드 리뷰 지연' 등은 흔히 보고되는 패턴을 가상 사례로 묘사한 것이며 특정 연구 수치를 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Pay engineers for tickets, and you'll get tickets
body: A product director at a large retailer gets a $60,000 pool to reward her twelve engineers this year. She wants the money to speed things up.
The obvious move is to pay for output. That's exactly where many engineering bonuses go wrong. This lesson puts two ideas from this unit to work: **when incentives backfire** and **fairness**.

image.label: An engineer splitting one big task card into many small ones
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 책상의 엔지니어가 큰 작업 카드 한 장을 가위로 잘게 잘라 작은 카드 여러 장으로 만들고, 옆의 동전 더미가 카드 수만큼 쌓여 가는 장면. 실제 회사 로고나 소프트웨어 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How should the pool be paid out?
body: The team builds checkout for the company's online store. Leadership cares about two things: fewer failed checkouts, and a new mobile checkout launching by autumn.

options.text: Pay each engineer per ticket closed
options.feedback: Easy to count, but engineers control the count. Tickets get split and untracked work like code review gets dropped. That's incentives backfiring.

options.text: Pay the whole team on failed checkouts and the launch date, with rules set in advance
options.feedback: Money follows results customers feel, which no one can game alone. Agreeing the rules up front also makes the payout feel fair later.

options.text: Let the director split it by her own ratings at year end
options.feedback: Judgment catches what numbers miss. But with no rules agreed beforehand, people may suspect favoritism. Fairness depends on the process, not just the result.

cards.title: Ticket bonuses move the count, not the work.
body: Picture option A after three months. One task becomes five tickets. Quick fixes beat careful ones because they close faster. Reviews pile up, since reviewing a colleague's code earns nothing. Bugs come back as fresh tickets, which also pay.
This is the pattern from **When incentives backfire**: when pay rides on a number people can move themselves, they move the number. The goal it was meant to measure gets left behind.

cards.title: The engineer who wrote −2000.
body: A story told by Apple engineer Andy Hertzfeld: in the early 1980s, managers on the Lisa computer team asked engineers to report how many lines of code they wrote each week.

That week, Bill Atkinson had rewritten part of the graphics code to be simpler and faster, cutting about 2,000 lines. He reportedly wrote **−2000** on the form. Within a few weeks, the story goes, managers stopped asking him to fill it in.
In engineering, the best work often makes things smaller. Output counts can't see that.

image.label: A weekly report form with -2000 written in the lines-of-code box
image.brief: 1980년대 느낌의 종이 주간 보고 양식 클로즈업. 'Lines of code this week' 칸에 손글씨로 크게 '−2000'. 옆에 짧아진 코드 출력물 한 장과 긴 출력물 더미 대비. 실제 회사 로고나 제품명은 넣지 않음.

cards.title: The launch lands. Who gets paid?
body: Mobile checkout ships on time, and failed checkouts drop. But it only worked because a separate platform team rebuilt the payment system first. They sit outside the director's budget.

options.text: Pay only the checkout team. It's their pool
options.feedback: Clean on paper, but the platform team sees their work rewarded in someone else's paycheck. People compare, and next time they'll guard their own priorities. That's fairness at work.

options.text: Pay the checkout team as promised, ask leadership to fund a share for the platform team, and add cross-team credit to next year's rules
options.feedback: You keep your promise and recognize the people who made the result possible. Fixing the rules for next year keeps the process fair, too.

options.text: Spread the same pool thinner to include both teams
options.feedback: Generous in spirit, but the checkout team was promised a pool under clear rules. Changing rules after the fact damages trust in the process.

cards.title: Team bonuses have their own costs.
body: Paying the whole team on shared results stops gaming, but it can hide a weak contributor and frustrate strong ones. Don't fix that by adding more counts to the bonus. Handle it through regular feedback and pay reviews.
No measure is perfect. Keep the formula simple, announce it early, and expect to adjust it next year rather than mid-year.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse.
body: You run a distribution center that fills orders for a chain of stores. You want a bonus to speed up picking. The day shift handles small, light orders. The night shift handles bulky ones.

options.text: Pay each picker per item picked, same rate on both shifts
options.feedback: Pickers will rush, and wrong items will reach stores. Night pickers also earn less for harder work. It fails on both backfire and fairness.

options.text: Pay each shift as a team on accurate orders shipped, adjusted for order size
options.feedback: Accuracy is built into what counts, so speed can't come at stores' expense. Adjusting for order size keeps the night shift's deal fair.

options.text: Pay per item picked, minus a penalty for each error found
options.feedback: The penalty closes the accuracy gap, but each picker still races alone, and the gap between shifts remains unfair.

cards.title: Check what you count, and who gets counted.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **When incentives backfire:** pay on results people can't move alone, not on outputs they can inflate. **Fairness:** set the rules before the work starts, and include everyone who made the result possible.
**Try it today:** take one bonus or target you run. Ask how someone could hit the number without helping the business, and who would feel left out when it pays.
